guides.title: Split, hooked or frayed brush tips
guides.summary: A tip that splits, bends or sprouts stray hairs can often be reshaped, and a few habits stop it happening again.
body: Work out which problem you have first. A split tip forks into two or more points. A hooked tip bends over to one side. A frayed tip has a few hairs poking out at odd angles. A splayed brush fans out from the metal collar. They have different causes, and only some can be fixed.

Most splits and splays come from paint drying up near the collar, which pushes the hairs apart from the inside. Pressing hard, scrubbing, stippling and jabbing into deep gaps do the same thing more slowly. Hooks usually come from a brush left resting on its tip, standing in the water pot or squashed in a case.

Try the gentle fix first. Wash the brush with brush soap, work a little lather into the hairs, shape a point with your fingers and let the soap dry in it overnight. Rinse it out the next day. Plenty of brushes that look ruined come back from this alone.

For a stubborn hook on a synthetic brush, dip just the hairs into water from a kettle that has stopped boiling, for two or three seconds. Shape the point straight away, then rinse in cold water to set it. Keep the collar out of the hot water, as heat softens the glue. Natural hair can be harmed by heat, so stick to the soap method on those.

A single stray hair can go. Snip it right at its base with a sharp craft blade or fine scissors, not halfway along. Never pull it out, as that loosens the hairs around it. If several hairs stray at once, the point is on its way out.

If paint has dried deep in the collar, soak only the hairs in brush restorer or isopropyl alcohol, then work it out with soap. It helps a little, but acrylic dried at the roots rarely comes out fully, and the point may never be quite as sharp again.

Prevention is mostly habit. Load only the front half of the hairs, rinse every few minutes, never leave a brush standing in water, and keep an old brush for drybrushing, glue and texture paste. Slide the cap back on only when the hairs are clean and lined up, or the cap itself bends the tip.

When a brush will not hold a point even after a soap reshape, retire it rather than fight it. It still has years of work left as a drybrush, a wash brush or a glue spreader. Mark the handle with a dab of paint so it does not creep back into your detail work.
keywords: brush won't come to a point

guides.title: How long to wait between coats
guides.summary: Thin acrylic coats are often ready in a few minutes, once the wet shine has gone and the paint no longer feels cool.
body: There is no single number. It depends on how thick the coat is, how warm and damp the room is, and what kind of paint it is. A thin layer on a warm day can be dry in two or three minutes. A thick coat on a cold, damp evening can take half an hour or more.

The easiest check is the shine. Wet acrylic looks glossy, and dry acrylic looks flat or satin. Tilt the model under your lamp and look for any wet sheen in the recesses, because that is where paint gathers and dries last.

Touch is the other check. Lightly touch a spot that does not matter, such as the underside of the base. If it feels cool or a little tacky, it is not dry. Wet paint also looks darker, so a colour that still seems to be shifting is still drying.

A rough guide for acrylics at room temperature: thin layers and edge highlights, a few minutes. Base coats, 10 to 15 minutes between coats. Washes and one-coat paints, 30 to 60 minutes, and longer where they pooled. Glazes need to be fully dry before the next one, as brushing over a damp glaze lifts it.

Going too early causes most of the trouble. The brush drags the soft paint below, leaving streaks, bald patches and a rough, gritty surface. A wash over a half-dry layer can lift it and leave a hole. If the brush suddenly feels sticky or draggy, stop and let it dry.

Touch dry is not the same as hard. Acrylic keeps hardening for a day or so. Leave a few hours before masking tape, heavy handling or varnish, and overnight if you can. Oils and enamels are far slower, and Drying and curing times for hobby products covers those.

You do not have to sit and wait. Move to another area or another model while the first dries, which is one reason batch painting suits beginners. A hair dryer on a cool setting speeds things up, and thinner coats dry faster anyway.

guides.title: Drying and curing times for hobby products
guides.summary: Paint dries in minutes, but primer, varnish, glue, putty and oils need far longer before they are safe to handle or paint over.
body: Dry and cured are not the same. Dry means the surface is no longer wet. Cured means the whole layer has hardened right through. Most products feel dry long before they are cured, and handling them too soon leaves fingerprints, dents and lifted paint.

Spray primer is usually touch dry in 15 to 30 minutes. Give it an hour or two before you paint over it, and overnight in cold or damp weather. Brushing onto soft primer can make it wrinkle or rub away. Primer put on with a brush is much the same.

Acrylic paint is touch dry in minutes and properly hard after about a day. Washes and one-coat paints that pooled want an hour or more. Before varnish, give the paint a few hours, and overnight is better.

Spray varnish is touch dry in well under an hour, and a second coat can go on once the first is. Leave the model a day before gaming with it or packing it into foam, as fresh varnish can pick up marks.

Plastic glue grips in minutes, sets firm in a few hours and reaches full strength in about a day. Superglue grabs in seconds and is solid within the hour. PVA holding sand on a base wants an hour or two before you tip off the loose grit, and overnight before priming.

Two-part putty usually stays workable for an hour or so and hardens over four or five hours; leave it overnight before sanding or priming, as thick fills stay soft inside. Texture paste and filler depend on thickness, from an hour for a thin smear to overnight for a deep layer.

Enamel washes and wipe-off effects stay workable for around half an hour and dry in a few hours to a day. Oil paint can stay workable for a day or more. Thin oil washes are often dry by the next day, but thicker oil work can take several days, so varnish only once a hidden spot is no longer tacky. Gentle warmth speeds both up a little.
Every product is different, so treat these as rough starting points and check the label. Cold, damp rooms slow everything down. When in doubt, leave it overnight; that is rarely the wrong call.

guides.title: First sessions: a path through Guides
guides.summary: A simple order for your first few weeks, naming the guides to read at each step so the long list never gets in the way.
body: Guides holds hundreds of entries, which is a lot when you are starting out. This is a short path through them. Each step names the guides to read, in order, and each step is roughly one evening at the table. If you want the whole picture first, Painting your first model walks through everything in one go.

Step one, get set up. Read A beginner's tool kit, Picking a model that is good to paint, Choosing hobby paints and Choosing brushes. You need far less than you might think: a few brushes, a handful of colours, a primer, cutters, a blade and some glue.

Step two, build and clean the model. Read Building your first plastic kit, Clipping parts off the sprue and Removing mould lines, then Cleaning and checking before priming. Time spent here shows through every coat that follows.
Step three, prime. Read Choosing a primer colour, then Spray priming, or Priming by brush if you have nowhere to spray. Let it dry properly before you go any further.

Step four, first colours. Read Thinning your paint, Using a wet palette, Base coating and How long to wait between coats. Thin coats, patience between them and a sharp brush point matter more than anything else at this stage, and Brush care and cleaning keeps that point.

Step five, shade and highlight. Read Applying a wash, then Drybrushing, then Edge highlighting or Layering. One wash and one highlight on each area is plenty for now. Order of painting explains which part to tackle first.

Step six, finish it. Read Painting the base rim and Varnishing models, and then call the model done. Common beginner mistakes and Perfectionism and fear of ruining a model are worth a read once you have a finished model to look back at.

After that, Base, wash and tidy method is a quick routine for your next few models, and What to learn next: a skill roadmap shows where to go when the basics feel easy. A handful of finished models teach more than one that never gets done.
keywords: how do i learn to paint minis

guides.title: Painting blue
guides.summary: Blue covers well and shades easily, so the real work is choosing warm or cool highlights and stopping it going chalky.
body: Blue is one of the friendlier colours. Most mid blues cover in a couple of thin coats over a grey or black undercoat, and dark blues go happily straight over black. Pale and sky blues are the exception: they are see-through, a bit like yellow, and want a white or light grey undercoat.

Decide early which way your blue leans. A blue with a touch of purple in it reads as rich and regal. A blue leaning towards green reads as teal, like deep sea water. Keep every step of the ladder leaning the same way, or the highlights look like a different paint.

Shade blue with a darker blue, a deep navy or a blue-black. A black wash suits blue better than most colours, but a dark blue or purple wash keeps the shadows richer. A brown wash turns blue greenish and dirty, which is fine for a weathered vehicle and not much else.

Highlighting is where blue goes wrong. White mixed straight in turns it powdery and pale very quickly. Add white in small steps, or highlight first with a lighter, brighter blue. A pale grey-blue or a touch of bone makes a softer top highlight than pure white.
Leaning the highlights helps too. For a crisp, cold look, push them towards a pale icy blue or a light turquoise. For a softer, older feel, add a drop of bone or pale skin tone instead.

A very dark blue makes a good stand-in for black. Navy cloth or armour with blue-grey edges reads as black on the table but has more life in it. If the finished steps look chalky, a thin glaze of the base blue pulls them back together.
Blue sits opposite orange, so copper, gold, warm leather and warm skin all look strong against it. For a calmer, colder look, pair it with greys and silver instead.

guides.title: Painting green
guides.summary: Decide whether your green leans yellow or blue, shade it with deeper greens and highlight with yellow rather than white.
body: Mid and dark greens cover fairly well, and dark greens go straight over black or grey. Bright yellow-greens behave more like yellow and want a light undercoat. A couple of thin coats beat one thick one, as ever.

Pick a direction. A green leaning yellow feels warm, natural and bright, like leaves and grass. A green leaning blue feels cold, deep and a little unnatural, like jade or sea water. Olive and khaki are greens with a lot of brown in them. Keep the whole ladder in one family.

Shade with a darker green, a blue-green or a dark brown-green. Black shadows can work on dark green, but they make a bright green look dead. A thin dark blue in the deepest recesses gives warm greens a cool, rich shadow.

Highlight by adding yellow or a pale yellow-green rather than white. White turns green minty and pastel fast. For the very top edges, a pale cream or bone keeps the colour without going chalky. On blue-greens, a pale turquoise works better than yellow.

Bright greens lose their punch as you highlight. A thin glaze of a vivid green or green ink over the finished area brings the colour back. On dark green armour, edge highlights in a lighter, slightly yellower green read clearly without many steps.
Olive and drab greens are forgiving and suit military kit. Base in olive, wash with brown, then highlight with olive mixed with bone or khaki. A little dust and chipping finishes them nicely.
Red sits opposite green, so red, pink and magenta accents look strong against it. Gold and brass trim looks warm and rich on dark green. For a natural feel, pair green with browns, leather and bone.

guides.title: Painting brown
guides.summary: Brown is really a dark orange, so shade it warm, highlight with tans and creams, and vary its warmth to keep parts apart.
body: Brown is easy to put on and harder to make interesting. Most browns cover well over any primer, and a brown wash flatters nearly everything. The danger is a model that ends up as one dull, muddy mass.

It helps to think of brown as a dark orange. Red-browns lean warm, like leather, chestnut or rust. Yellow-browns lean towards ochre and tan. Grey-browns and olive-browns are cooler and feel older or dirtier. Choosing which one you want makes every later step easier.
Shade with a darker brown, a dark red-brown or a brown-black. Pure black shadows can look grey and dull on warm browns. A thin dark red-brown in the recesses keeps leather and wood looking rich.

Highlight with tan, a sandy beige or a bone colour rather than pure white. White in brown turns pinkish grey and chalky quickly. On leather, a light orange-brown highlight looks warm and worn. On wood, keep the highlights paler and duller, and follow the grain.

If a brown looks flat, give it a direction. A thin orange glaze makes it warmer and fresher. A thin green or grey glaze makes it older and colder. A little of the model's main colour glazed into the shadows ties it in with everything else.

On a model with lots of brown parts, separate them by value and warmth. Put a dark brown next to a light one, and a red-brown next to an olive-brown. Telling browns and leathers apart goes into this in more depth.
Blue and teal sit opposite the orange in brown, so they make browns glow. Brown also sits well with greens, cream and bone for a natural, earthy scheme.

guides.title: Painting grey
guides.summary: Plain grey looks unfinished, so lean it warm or cool, shade with tinted darks and keep the brightest highlights small.
body: Most models start out grey, which is why a plain grey paint job can look unfinished. The trick is to make it look chosen: give it a lean, a clear light and dark, and something colourful next to it.

Choose warm or cool. A blue-grey feels clean, cold and hard, which suits armour, stone and machines. A brown-grey or green-grey feels warm, aged and earthy, which suits cloth, old stone and ash. Tinting whites, greys and blacks covers mixing these.

Shade grey with a wash that matches its lean: dark blue or black for cool greys, brown or sepia for warm ones. A black wash on a warm grey can look dirty, which is great for grime and wrong for clean cloth.

Highlight by adding white in small steps and keeping the tint in every mix. A cool grey can finish with a very pale blue, and a warm grey with bone or cream. Keep the lightest steps to the sharpest edges and top surfaces, or the whole area goes chalky.

Grey hides value problems, so check for them. Mid grey armour next to mid grey stone and mid grey metal merges into one blob. Push one part darker and another lighter, or change the tint, so each one reads.
Grey makes other colours look brighter. A small red, orange or yellow accent jumps out against grey armour or stone, which makes grey a strong main colour for a model with one bright feature.
For grey hair, skin and fur, the detail recipes White and grey hair, Grey undead skin and Grey hide give full steps. For armour, Grey and blue-grey armour is the one to open.

guides.title: Painting horses and mounts
guides.summary: Paint mount and rider apart, give the coat a believable colour and keep the tack plain so the rider still stands out.
body: If you can, paint the horse and rider separately and glue them together at the end. Most riders hide part of the saddle and the horse's back, and reaching between a leg and a flank with a brush is no fun. Put the rider on its own handle or cork while you work.

Pick a real coat colour, because everyone knows roughly what horses look like. Chestnut is an even red-brown all over, with a mane the same colour or paler. Bay is a red or dark brown body with a black mane, tail and lower legs. Black horses look best with blue-grey highlights. Greys run from dark and dappled to nearly white.

A horse's coat is short and glossy, not fluffy. Rather than heavy drybrushing, shade with a wash and layer the highlights over the big muscles: shoulder, hip, neck and the top of the head. Save drybrushing for shaggy ponies and hairy beasts.

Manes and tails are where the texture goes. Paint long strokes that follow the hair, darker at the roots and lighter on the strands that catch the light. A black mane and tail are quick and look smart on most coat colours.

Paint white face marks and socks over a pale grey first so the white covers in one or two coats. Keep their edges soft rather than outlined, and vary them from horse to horse so a unit does not look cloned.

Hooves are a dark grey-brown, or a pale horn colour under white socks. Eyes are dark brown or black with a tiny light dot. The nose and lips are dark and a little shiny; a dab of gloss varnish there looks good up close.

Keep the tack simple: dark brown leather for the saddle and straps, metal for the buckles and bit, and perhaps one coloured saddle cloth. Make that cloth the rider's main colour so horse and rider read as one model.

Monster mounts follow the same thinking. Decide which real animal they are closest to and borrow its colours and markings, then keep the beast a little duller than its rider so the eye goes to the figure on top.

guides.title: Using Colour Lab
guides.summary: Colour Lab, in the Painting tab, helps you find paints that go together, plan a scheme and find a near match among your paints.
body: Colour Lab lives in the Painting tab. It has five parts, picked from the row of buttons at the top: Wheel, Colour ideas, Colour plans, Colours you've used and Paint Picker. Wherever it suggests paints, your own come first.

Wheel lays out your paints and the built-in paints by colour. Tap a colour to see what is in it, then a group to see its paints from dark to light. It is a quick way to spot which colours you have plenty of and which you are missing.

Colour ideas starts from one paint. Choose it in the Start from box, then say what you are painting, such as trim, gems, or eyes and glow. You get three paints that go with it, each with a short reason and a fit: Good, Okay or Poor, judged by how close the colour is.

Colour plans are ready-made sets of colours that work together, grouped by theme or by combination. They have colours but no steps. When one appeals, save it into a new recipe and add the steps there.
Colours you've used looks back through your own saved recipes for units of the same faction and lists the paints you used most. It helps a new unit match the ones you painted months ago.

Paint Picker takes a base colour, a second colour if you want one, and a part: armour, eyes, weapon or base. It gives up to three paints for each colour, with the reason. The Paint Picker chip in Mentor opens it too.

Most paint rows have Use in a recipe, Add to a recipe and Similar paints. Similar paints shows the closest matches, a lighter and a darker option, your closest owned paint, and sometimes a mix of two of your paints to try. A paint you do not own can go on your shopping list.

Colours on a screen are a guide, not a promise. Screens differ, and paint dries a little darker than it looks wet. Try a suggestion on a swatch card or a spare part before you commit a whole model to it.
keywords: how do i use colour lab

guides.title: Mixing paints from different makers
guides.summary: Water-based hobby acrylics from different makers mix and layer together fine, but keep solvent paints apart and test first.
body: Most hobby paints are water-based acrylics, whatever the label says. They mix on the palette, layer over each other and thin with water in the same way. Painting one model with paints from three or four makers is completely normal.

They do feel different. Some are thicker and need more water, some are runnier and dry with more sheen, and some carry more pigment and cover in one coat. When you mix two together, the runnier one may mean you need less water than usual.
Paints with different finishes can leave a patchy sheen, part matt and part satin. It is rarely a real problem, and a coat of matt varnish at the end evens it out.

Keep solvent paints apart. Enamels, lacquers and oils do not mix with acrylics in the pot or on the palette. Enamel washes and oils can go over fully dry acrylic, which is how most weathering works. Lacquer sprayed over acrylic is riskier and can wrinkle it. Acrylic over a fully cured lacquer or enamel layer is usually fine.

Metallic, one-coat and special paints mix too, with care. A drop of metallic in a normal colour spreads a metal sparkle through the whole mix, which is hard to control. One-coat paints keep their flow better when thinned with their own medium than with lots of water. Texture and crackle paints are best used on their own.
Washes and inks from different makers can be mixed into a new shade. Mix a small amount on the palette and try it on a spare part first, as some inks are far stronger than others.
If a mix turns lumpy, stringy or forms a skin straight away, stop and use something else. That is rare with acrylics and usually means one of the paints is old or not acrylic at all.

guides.title: Matching a colour you have run out of
guides.summary: When a pot runs dry or stops being made, find a near match by eye, by swatch or in Colour Lab, then test it on a spare part.
body: It happens to everyone. Halfway through a unit the pot dries up, or the colour is no longer made. You rarely need an exact match. On the table, a colour that is close in lightness and warmth will pass, especially once a wash and highlights go over it.

Start with what you have. If you wrote the recipe down, you know the name, and a swatch card shows the dried colour. If not, a finished model is the best sample. Look at it under your painting lamp rather than a ceiling light.

In Colour Lab, find the old paint and open Similar paints. Best match lists close paints from other makers, Your closest shows the nearest ones you own, and Try mixing may suggest a blend of two of your paints with the parts to use. Treat it as a starting point, as screens are never perfect.

To mix a match by hand, start from the paint closest in colour and change one thing at a time. Too bright: add a touch of grey or of the opposite colour. Too warm: a little blue. Too cool: a little red or yellow. Too dark: a lighter paint from the same family rather than white, which turns it chalky.
Paint the test on a spare part or the underside of a base, let it dry, and hold it next to the original under the same light. Wet paint looks darker and glossier, so only judge it once it is dry.
Once it matches, mix enough for the whole job and keep it in a spare dropper bottle or a sealed pot. Write the ratio into your recipe so you can make it again.

If it is close but not perfect, hide the join. Switch paint at a natural break, such as a new model or a new panel, rather than halfway across a cloak. A shared wash or glaze over old and new areas also pulls them together.
keywords: paint dried up in the pot
